title: Trends in low back pain burden attributable to high BMI and occupational ergonomic factors among women in four selected Asia–Pacific Subregions, 1990–2023
content:
by Xiang Xiao, Yuxue Xiao, Ruizhe Li, Zebiao Zheng, Yipu Xiao, Hang Ren

Background

Low back pain (LBP) is a major cause of disability worldwide. We investigated the burden of female LBP attributable to high body mass index (BMI) and occupational ergonomic factors across four Asia–Pacific subregions.

Methods

Using Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 data, we assessed disability–adjusted life years (DALYs) and DALY rates in East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Oceania from 1990 to 2023. Joinpoint regression, socioeconomic inequality, decomposition, and frontier analyses were performed, and Bayesian age–period–cohort models projected burden through 2040.

Results

High–BMI–attributable LBP burden increased across all four subregions, with South Asia showing the most pronounced increase. In 2023, the high–BMI–attributable age–standardized DALY rate (ASDR) was 78.66 per 100,000 in South Asia and was projected to reach 98.71 by 2040 (95% credible interval (CrI), 36.50–160.93). Occupational–ergonomic–factor–attributable ASDRs declined from 1990 to 2023 in East and South Asia but increased in Southeast Asia and Oceania. By 2040, occupational–attributable ASDRs were projected to decline to 76.15 in East Asia (95% CrI, 14.34–137.96) and 123.62 in Southeast Asia (95% CrI, 83.30–163.94), while remaining relatively stable in Oceania at 128.20 (95% CrI, 75.16–181.24). For both risk factors, burden was concentrated in middle age. Socioeconomic gradients were uncertain by 2023, and decomposition analysis showed that epidemiological change was the largest contributor to increasing high–BMI–attributable DALYs in South and Southeast Asia, whereas population growth contributed substantially to occupational–attributable DALYs.

Conclusions

The two attributable burdens showed different temporal, demographic, and projected patterns across the four subregions. Prevention priorities may therefore need to reflect local risk profiles and demographic context.
